activity: I-tsing's port of departure. Having failed to keep his companions, in the 11th month of 671 he embarked at Kwang-tung on a Persian merchant ship to sail south for India, the patronage of the Fêng family supplying his needs. He returned here in 689 to seek paper, ink and scribes for copying the scriptures gathered at Śrībhoga.

activity: The great Buddhist hub of the Southern Sea and I-tsing's base on both the outward and homeward legs. Twenty days' sail from Canton he reached Bhoga, landed and stayed six months learning Sanskrit grammar; the king sent him on to Malayu (which had by then 'become Bhoga'). In the fortified city of Bhoga more than a thousand priests studied just as in India, and I-tsing urged China-bound pilgrims to train here first. He returned here after his Indian years to translate and compile this very Record, its priests almost all of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, with a few Mahāyānists in Malayu.
features: mostly Mūlasarvāstivāda; a few Mahāyānists in Malayu

activity: Islands passed on the crossing to India, more than ten days' sail north from Ka-cha. The shore was lined with coconut and betel-nut forest; the naked, medium-built islanders paddled out by the hundred in little boats to barter coconuts, bananas and rattan-ware, prizing only iron — five to ten coconuts for a finger-sized piece — and they would loose poisoned arrows on any who refused to trade.

anecdotes.title: The iron-hungry islanders
anecdotes.summary: The naked islanders would trade five to ten coconuts for a scrap of iron the size of two fingers, refusing offered clothes; a single poisoned arrow was said to prove fatal to any who declined to barter.

activity: I-tsing's landfall in India and the gateway of his pilgrimage, the southern limit of Eastern India, forty yojanas from the eastern frontier and some sixty from Mahābodhi and Nālandā. He arrived on the 8th day of the 2nd month of 673, stayed about a year studying Sanskrit with the master Mahāyānapradīpa (a pupil of Xuanzang), and set out west with him and many merchants. It is also where he re-embarked for home. There are five or six monasteries and the people are rich.

activity: The centre of I-tsing's Indian sojourn, where he lived and studied for about ten years (c. 675–685), worshipping the Root Temple (Mūlagandhakuṭī). Much of the Record's detail on monastic discipline — the assignment of rooms each year, the daily rules — is drawn from what he observed at Nālandā, which he holds up as the model of correct practice.

scholarlyNotes.notes: The same Nālandā Mahāvihāra where Xuanzang studied a generation earlier. Coordinates are in data/canonical/places.json. activity: The place of the Buddha's enlightenment, which I-tsing reached after Nālandā and the Vulture Peak. He worshipped 'the image of the real face' of the Buddha, and offered it a kāṣāya robe of the Tathāgata's own size made from silks entrusted to him by the priests and laity of Shan-tung. He records that the Mahābodhi monastery adhered to the Sthavira school yet also belonged to the Mahāyāna.

monasteries.text: the Deer Park monastery, and near it the ruined Chinese (Chih-na) monastery of King Śrī-Gupta

activity: A monastery on the Ganges about forty yojanas downstream (east) of Nālandā, recorded in I-tsing's Kao Seng Chuan. Near it lay the ruined foundations of the Chih-na — 'Chinese' — monastery, built by King Śrī-Gupta some five hundred years earlier for monks who had come from China via Sichuan, and endowed with twenty-four villages. By I-tsing's century the Chinese monks were long dead and only three villages remained with the Deer Park monastery; the king of Eastern India, Devavarman, was said to be willing to restore the temple and its land if pilgrim monks came again from China.

anecdotes.title: The lost Chinese monastery of King Śrī-Gupta
anecdotes.summary: Some five hundred years earlier, more than twenty Chinese monks reached the Mahābodhi via Sichuan; King Śrī-Gupta built them the Chih-na ('Chinese') monastery and endowed it with twenty-four villages. After the monks died the monastery fell to ruin and the land passed to others — but King Devavarman of Eastern India offered to return the temple and its villages should monks come again from the land of the Son of Heaven.

features: forty yojanas east of Nālandā, down the Ganges

date.basis: Described in the Kao Seng Chuan alongside the Nālandā account, i.e. during I-tsing's Indian years (673–685); the visit it records cannot be dated more precisely.

scholarlyNotes.notes: Despite its Chinese name Lü-yüan ('Deer Park'), this is not Sārnāth: the text places it forty yojanas east of Nālandā down the Ganges. Foucher identified it with the Mṛgasthāpana stūpa of Varendrabhumi (northern Bengal). 'The pilgrim' whose visit the passage describes may be I-ching himself or the monk whose biography hosts it (Hui-lun), so the entry is marked as reported rather than firsthand. Lahiri notes the King Devavarman mentioned may be Devakhadga of the Khadga dynasty of Samataṭa.
